start: Thy business is with the action only
context: Spoken to the warrior Arjuna, paralysed by doubt before battle. One of the Gita's central teachings: act fully and well, but release your grip on the result.
prompt: Where are you waiting for a guaranteed outcome before you allow yourself to begin?

start: The contacts of matter
context: Arjuna is reminded that sensations and moods arise and pass like the seasons. Steadiness comes from not mistaking a passing state for the whole of who we are.
prompt: Which feeling right now would you hold more lightly if you remembered it will pass?

start: Better one's own duty
context: The Gita's idea of svadharma: each person has their own path. Living one's own life imperfectly is better than imitating someone else's perfectly.
prompt: Whose life have you been measuring yours against?

start: Let him raise the self by the Self
context: We are asked to lift ourselves up through our own effort. The same mind that can drag us down can also be our closest ally.
prompt: Have you been your own friend or your own enemy this week?

start: The good is one thing, the pleasant another
context: Spoken by Death to the young seeker Nachiketas, who has refused every pleasure offered him in exchange for real understanding.
prompt: Where are the good and the pleasant pulling you in different directions?

start: As a man, casting off worn-out garments
context: The Gita teaches that the deepest self is not destroyed with the body. Whatever one believes about rebirth, the image invites us to see change as renewal.
prompt: What 'worn-out garment' in your life are you ready to lay aside?

start: For certain is death for the born
context: Not a dismissal of grief, but a reminder that the cycle of life and death is the most certain thing there is.
prompt: What inevitable change are you still resisting?

start: He whose mind
context: A portrait of the 'sthitaprajna', the person of steady wisdom: undisturbed by pain, unseduced by pleasure, free of fear and anger.
prompt: What unsettles your mind most easily?

parts: Man, musing on the objects of sense
context: A precise chain of cause and effect: dwelling leads to attachment, attachment to desire, desire to anger, and anger to the loss of clear thinking.
prompt: What have you been dwelling on that could start this chain?

start: He attaineth Peace, into whom all desires flow
context: The ocean receives every river yet stays the same. Peace is not the absence of desires but not being moved by them.
prompt: Which desire could you let flow in without letting it move you?

start: When, again, as a tortoise
context: The tortoise draws in its limbs when it needs to. The wise can likewise withdraw from the pull of the senses at will.
prompt: When did you last withdraw, deliberately, from all the noise?

start: therefore cleave thou to yoga
context: One of the Gita's most famous definitions. Yoga here is not posture but a way of acting: skilful, balanced and free of grasping.
prompt: What would it mean to act with real skill today?

start: Nor can anyone, even for an instant, remain really actionless
context: Even doing nothing is a kind of action. The question is never whether to act, but how.
prompt: What are you 'doing' even when you think you are doing nothing?

start: Perform thou right
context: Krishna urges Arjuna out of paralysis. Withdrawal from life is not the answer; right action is.
prompt: Where has hesitation become a kind of inaction?

start: Whatsoever a great man doeth
context: Example teaches more than instruction. Those whom others look up to carry a particular responsibility.
prompt: Who is watching how you live, and what are they learning?

start: It is desire, it is wrath
context: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong even against their will. The answer: desire and its companion, anger.
prompt: Where have desire or anger acted through you lately?

start: Verily there is no purifier in this world like wisdom
context: Understanding, more than ritual, is what transforms a person.
prompt: What understanding has changed you most?

start: Sages look equally on
context: A radical statement of equality in its time: the wise see the same essence in a learned priest, an animal and a person society rejects.
prompt: Whom do you find it hardest to see as equal?

parts: Verily yoga is not for him who eateth too much
context: The path is one of moderation: neither indulgence nor extreme austerity, in food, sleep, work or play.
prompt: Where in your daily rhythm is balance missing?

start: As a lamp in a windless place
context: A classic image of a concentrated mind: a flame so sheltered it does not flicker.
prompt: What winds make your mind flicker?

start: As often as the wavering and unsteady mind
context: Meditation is not never wandering; it is coming back, as many times as it takes.
prompt: Can you be patient with your mind each time it wanders?

parts: as hard to curb as the wind.
context: Arjuna complains that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees, and offers two remedies: practice and letting go.
prompt: What practice could steady your mind, a little each day?

start: Humility, unpretentiousness, harmlessness
context: Part of a list of qualities the Gita calls true knowledge. Wisdom shows itself as character.
prompt: Which of these qualities would you like to grow in?

context: From a list of the 'divine qualities' a person can cultivate.
prompt: Which of these is most alive in you, and which least?

start: Triple is the gate of this hell
context: Lust, anger and greed are named as the three doors to self-destruction.
prompt: Which of the three doors stands most open in your life?

start: Speech causing no annoyance
context: The Gita describes an 'austerity of speech': words that are true, kind and helpful at once.
prompt: Were your words today truthful, pleasant and beneficial?

parts: Which at first is as venom
That which from the union of the senses
context: Two kinds of pleasure: one bitter at first and sweet in the end, the other sweet at first and bitter in the end.
prompt: Which of your pleasures are venom first, and which nectar first?

start: Whoso forsaketh all desires
context: Peace comes not from getting what we want but from being free of the craving and the ego that drive us.
prompt: What yearning could you set down, even for an hour?

parts: Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot
He who has no understanding and whose mind
like good horses of a charioteer.
context: One of the most famous images in Indian philosophy. The senses are horses; the mind is the reins; understanding is the driver.
prompt: Who is driving your chariot today: the horses or the charioteer?

start: Rise, awake!
context: A call to wakefulness. The path to self-knowledge is as narrow as a razor's edge, which is exactly why it needs attention.
prompt: What are you being called to wake up to?

start: Fools dwelling in darkness
end: blind men led by the blind
context: Death warns Nachiketas about people who mistake cleverness for wisdom.
prompt: Whom are you following, and can they see the way?

start: The Self-existent pierced the openings
context: Our senses face outward, so we naturally look outward. The Upanishad invites the rarer turn inward.
prompt: What would you see if you closed your eyes and looked within?

start: The true prevails, not the untrue
context: The first words, 'Satyameva jayate', are India's national motto.
prompt: Where do you need to trust that truth will prevail?

start: Two birds, inseparable friends
context: One bird tastes the fruits of life, sweet and bitter; the other simply watches. Many read them as two sides of ourselves: the one who experiences and the one who witnesses.
prompt: Can you be, for a moment, the bird that only watches?

start: And he who beholds all beings in the Self
context: The Isha Upanishad's vision of unity: when we see ourselves in others and others in ourselves, the walls that cause sorrow fall away.
prompt: Whom could you see as part of yourself today?

start: When thou hast surrendered all this
context: A paradox at the opening of the Isha Upanishad: we enjoy most fully what we no longer try to possess.
prompt: What could you enjoy more by holding it less tightly?

parts: That which is the subtile essence
context: A father teaches his son Svetaketu by dissolving salt in water: invisible, yet present in every sip. 'Thou art that' (tat tvam asi) is one of the great sayings of the Upanishads.
prompt: What is present in your life even though you cannot see it?

start: The Infinite (bhûman)
context: The sage Sanatkumara teaches that no finite thing can bring lasting joy.
prompt: What finite thing have you been expecting to make you whole?

start: I have heard from men like you, that he who knows the Self
context: The learned Narada has mastered every science, yet comes to his teacher in grief. Knowledge of things, he discovers, is not knowledge of oneself.
prompt: What do you know about the world that you have not yet learned about yourself?

start: He is not born, nor doth he die
context: Krishna speaks of the innermost self, which the Gita holds to be untouched by birth and death.
prompt: What in you feels unchanged since you were a child?
